analysis.one_liner: Raises taxes on the highest incomes and corporations while expanding tax credits and benefits for working families.
analysis.headline: After passing the House 218-216 and the Senate 51-50 on the Vice President's tie-breaking vote, with no Republican support in either chamber, it was signed into law on August 10, 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This was the 1993 deficit-reduction package. It raised income-tax rates on the highest earners, raised corporate taxes, and reduced Medicare payments to providers, using the revenue and savings to shrink the deficit. At the same time it expanded the Earned Income Tax Credit for low-wage workers, loosened food stamp rules, replaced bank-guaranteed student loans with cheaper direct federal loans, and paid for free childhood vaccines. It became law without a single Republican vote in either chamber.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-wage working families get bigger Earned Income Tax Credit checks [S4]; food stamp households get easier rules and higher deductions [S4]; students and parents get direct federal loans at lower interest rates and lower fees, with income-contingent repayment [S4]; uninsured, Medicaid, and Indian children get federally purchased free vaccines [S4]. Long-covered retirees get a phased-in reduction in the Medicare Part A premium [S4]. The Treasury gains revenue from high earners and corporations, and all taxpayers share in reduced deficit borrowing [S4].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-wage workers, food stamp households, students, children

how_it_helps.text: Expanded the Earned Income Tax Credit — a refundable credit that pays cash to low-wage workers — by revising credit and phaseout percentages for 1994.

Made food stamps more generous: removed the cap on the shelter deduction, excluded the tax credit from counted income for a year after receipt, raised dependent-care deductions and vehicle limits, and simplified applications.

Created the Federal Direct Student Loan Program, replacing the program in which private banks made government-guaranteed loans, phased in over five years, with lower interest rates, lower origination fees, and income-contingent repayment options.
Required Medicaid programs to distribute federally purchased pediatric vaccines to eligible children at no charge, with outreach and education to raise immunization rates.

Raised marginal rates and imposed a surtax on the highest incomes, made permanent the limits on itemized deductions and the phaseout of personal exemptions for high earners, raised the top estate-and-gift tax rate, and raised the corporate rate on income above $10 million.
Capped the corporate tax deduction for employee pay above $1 million, denied deductions for lobbying expenses and social club dues, and required securities dealers to mark positions to market.
Extended pay-as-you-go budget rules through fiscal 1998 and increased the debt limit to carry out the plan.
Phased in a reduction of the Medicare Part A premium for individuals with 30 or more quarters of coverage and their spouses.

analysis.who_pays: Households with the highest incomes pay higher rates, a surtax, and a higher estate-and-gift tax rate [S4]. Corporations pay a higher rate on income above $10 million and face new limits on deductions [S4]. Hospitals, doctors, nursing homes, home health agencies, labs, and medical equipment suppliers absorb lower or frozen Medicare payment updates [S4]. Drivers and shippers pay higher motor-fuels taxes [S4]. Federal retirees wait three extra months for cost-of-living adjustments [S4]. Veterans pay higher VA home-loan fees, and survivors' benefits lose half their 1994 adjustment [S4]. Families of nursing-home residents face estate recovery and asset-transfer limits [S4].
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners, corporations, Medicare providers, drivers, federal retirees

drawbacks.text: Raised excise taxes on gasoline, diesel, aviation fuel, and compressed natural gas, which raises costs for every driver and shipper, not just the wealthy.

Required states to recover nursing-home costs from the estates of Medicaid beneficiaries and delayed eligibility for people who transferred assets for less than market value, shifting costs onto some middle-class families.

Cut or froze Medicare payment updates for hospitals, skilled nursing facilities, home health agencies, labs, and equipment suppliers; benefits were untouched, but payment pressure falls hardest on rural and small providers.

Repealed the luxury tax on boats, aircraft, jewelry, and furs, made the low-income housing credit and mortgage bond programs permanent with passive-loss relief for real estate investors, and extended the research credit — breaks for well-off buyers and developers inside a bill framed as shared sacrifice.
Delayed federal retirement cost-of-living adjustments by three months, cut the 1994 survivors' benefit adjustment in half for veterans, and raised VA home-loan fees.
Barred state and local governments from imposing rate or entry regulation on mobile phone service, removing consumer price oversight even as carriers gained FCC cost-recovery fees.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core exchange is progressive: tax increases concentrated on the highest incomes and corporations pay for credits and benefits that flow to working families and to future taxpayers through deficit reduction. The regressions — the fuel tax, Medicaid estate recovery, provider payment cuts, and the luxury-goods and real-estate repeals — are real but secondary. The bill survived by margins of one and two votes with unanimous Republican opposition, which reflects how much both parties' coalitions had to swallow to pass it.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House 218-216 and the Senate 51-50, with the Vice President's tie-breaking vote needed in the Senate, and the President signed it on August 10, 1993.

narrative.text: The House Budget Committee reported the reconciliation bill as an original measure on May 25, 1993, and the House passed it 219-213 on May 27 — every Democrat but 38 voting yes, all 175 Republicans voting no.
The Senate passed its own amended version 50-49 on June 25, with the Vice President casting the deciding vote; all 43 voting Republicans opposed it.
In conference, the House's broad energy tax based on the heat content (Btu) of fuels was dropped in favor of increases in motor-fuels taxes.
The House adopted the conference report 218-216 on August 5, and the Senate agreed 51-50 on August 6-7, again on the Vice President's tie-breaking vote.
The President signed it on August 10, 1993; it became Public Law 103-66.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Working families gained the expanded tax credit, food stamp relief, direct student loans, and free vaccines; the Treasury gained revenue from high earners, corporations, and providers. Luxury-goods sellers and real estate interests also won tax repeals and permanent credits tucked into the package.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Working families; Treasury; luxury and real estate interests

for.name: Bill Clinton
for.what_they_did: Championed the deficit-reduction package and signed it into law on August 10, 1993.

for.name: Martin Olav Sabo
for.what_they_did: Reported the original measure, managed its floor consideration, and brought up the conference report in the House.

for.name: Richard Gephardt
for.what_they_did: Served as a House conferee on the Budget panel and voted for final passage.

for.name: Al Gore
for.what_they_did: Cast the tie-breaking votes in the Senate on June 25 and again on final passage August 6-7.

for.name: 217 of 258 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on the conference report (218-216); 218 had voted yes on the bill in May.

for.name: 50 of 56 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on final Senate passage; six voted no.

against.name: 175 of 176 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on both the bill (219-213) and the conference report (218-216); not one supported final passage.

against.name: 44 of 44 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on the Senate bill (50-49) and unanimously against the conference report (51-50).

against.name: Bob Dole
against.what_they_did: Led the Senate Republicans' unanimous opposition to the package.

against.name: John Kasich
against.what_they_did: Offered a spending-cut substitute and motions to instruct conferees to reject any increases in direct spending.

against.name: Energy-intensive manufacturers and oil and gas interests
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against the proposed Btu energy tax, which was dropped in conference in favor of motor-fuels taxes.

sides.party_line_note: No Republican in either chamber voted for final passage — 0 of 175 House Republicans and 0 of 44 Senate Republicans — while 217 of 258 House Democrats and 50 of 56 Senate Democrats voted yes, and the Vice President broke the Senate tie.

industries.industry: Hospitals, physicians, and nursing homes (Medicare providers)
industries.note: Payment updates for hospitals, nursing facilities, home health agencies, labs, and physicians were reduced or frozen; benefits themselves were untouched, so the industry's revenue loss funds deficit reduction.

industries.industry: Student loan lenders (banks, guaranty agencies, Sallie Mae)
industries.note: Direct federal lending replaces the guaranteed-loan program over five years; lenders face offset and transfer fees, lower tax exemptions, and reduced reinsurance.

industries.industry: Luxury goods makers (boats, aircraft, jewelry, furs)
industries.note: The 1990 luxury excise tax on their products was repealed; the tax had been paid by wealthy buyers.

The low-income housing credit and mortgage bond programs became permanent and passive-loss limits were relaxed; the credit keeps private developers as the channel for subsidized housing while the relief benefits investors.
They gained exemption from state and local rate and entry regulation and FCC cost-recovery fees, but must bid competitively for spectrum licenses.
The broad Btu energy tax in the House bill was dropped, but excise taxes on gasoline, diesel, and aviation fuels rose.
States may run Medicaid drug formularies and the rebate inflation formula was repealed, but new drugs are shielded from prior-authorization controls for their first six months.

industries.industry: Mining claim holders on federal land
industries.note: Unpatented mining claims now carry an annual maintenance fee (about $100 per claim) and a location fee in place of assessment work.
